title: Maximum Product Subarray
description: Like Kadane's, but a negative number can flip the smallest (most-negative) product into the new maximum — so you must track BOTH the max and min ending at the current index.

conversation.intro: How an interview about this problem would actually play out. Each section has two parts: what you'd actually say out loud, and why that move matters. Tap a section to expand.

sections.title: 1. Restate & clarify
sections.prompt: Before touching code — pin down the inputs.
sections.say:
"Let me restate: given an integer array `nums`, return the largest product of any *contiguous non-empty subarray*. Contiguous means adjacent in the array; non-empty means we have to pick at least one element."

Then a few quick clarifying questions:
• Confirming contiguous (subarray), not subsequence — affects the recurrence shape entirely.
• Are negatives and zeros both possible? (They are — that's what makes this harder than max-sum.)
• Is the array guaranteed non-empty? Should I throw or return something specific on empty input?
• Can values be floats, or integers only? (Floats add precision concerns.)
• Return value — just the max product, or also the subarray itself?
sections.why: The contiguous question is the load-bearing clarification — if it were subsequence, you'd want to multiply all positives plus an even count of the most-negative values, a totally different algorithm. Confirming negatives are present is what justifies needing TWO rolling vars (max and min); without negatives, plain Kadane on the product would work. The non-empty guarantee pins down the seed: initialize `best = nums[0]` so a single-element array trivially works.

sections.title: 2. Brute force first (out loud)
sections.prompt: Name the obvious O(n²) solution before you discard it.
sections.say: "The brute force is two nested loops: outer picks the start index `i`, inner walks `j` from `i` to the end multiplying as it goes, tracking the global max product. That's `O(n²)` time, `O(1)` space. Correct, but we can drop it to `O(n)` if we figure out how to keep just enough state per index to extend without restarting."
sections.why: Naming the `O(n²)` brute force out loud establishes the comparison baseline. The win in section 3 — `O(n)` time with two rolling vars — looks like magic without it. It also surfaces the question that motivates the trick: 'what's the minimum state I need to extend the running product through a new element?' Answer: the best AND worst product ending at the previous index, because a negative can flip them.

sections.title: 3. Spot the pattern
sections.prompt: What signal in the problem points to a two-track Kadane variant?
sections.say:
"This is a Kadane-shaped 1D DP, but with a twist: I need to track *both* the max AND min product ending at each index. The reason is the negative-number flip — at index `i`, multiplying by a negative number takes whatever the worst (most-negative) running product was and flips it into the new biggest positive. So the recurrence is:
• `maxHere[i] = max(nums[i], maxHere[i-1] * nums[i], minHere[i-1] * nums[i])`
• `minHere[i] = min(nums[i], maxHere[i-1] * nums[i], minHere[i-1] * nums[i])`

The three candidates are: (a) start fresh at `nums[i]` (resets after a zero or a wrong-sign run), (b) extend the running max product, (c) extend the running min product (which may now be the biggest because of a negative flip).

Global answer `best = max(best, maxHere[i])` across all `i`. Two scalars suffice — drop to `O(1)` space. The critical implementation detail: compute candMax and candMin from the SAME (old) maxHere/minHere before assigning either back. If you overwrite maxHere first, candMin sees the new value and computes the wrong product."
sections.why: The negative-flip insight is the entire load-bearing pedagogy of this problem — without it, candidates write single-track Kadane and silently fail on `[-2, 3, -4]`. Articulating *why* min needs tracking ('a negative turns the worst into the best') is what shows real DP intuition, not just memorization. The 'start fresh at nums[i]' candidate handles the zero-reset case implicitly — no need for a `if (nums[i] === 0)` branch, the max/min recurrence handles it. The same-source-before-assign warning is the gotcha that the interviewer will probe.

sections.title: 4. Trace through examples
sections.prompt: Walk a few inputs to confirm the model before writing the loop.
sections.intro: "Let me trace through a couple of cases to make sure my model is right." Three inputs cover the interesting behaviors — the typical mixed case, a zero-reset, and the case where the whole array is the answer because two negatives cancel.

examples.note: Canonical case — the best subarray is [2, 3] with product 6. The -2 then 4 don't get to 6, and including them would multiply through the -2.
examples.trace:
seed: maxHere=2, minHere=2, best=2
i=1 x=3:
  candMax = max(3, 2*3=6, 2*3=6) = 6
  candMin = min(3, 6, 6) = 3
  maxHere=6, minHere=3, best=max(2,6)=6
i=2 x=-2:
  candMax = max(-2, 6*-2=-12, 3*-2=-6) = -2
  candMin = min(-2, -12, -6) = -12
  maxHere=-2, minHere=-12, best=max(6,-2)=6
i=3 x=4:
  candMax = max(4, -2*4=-8, -12*4=-48) = 4
  candMin = min(4, -8, -48) = -48
  maxHere=4, minHere=-48, best=max(6,4)=6
return 6

examples.note: Zero resets — the 'start fresh at nums[i]' candidate ensures the 0 wipes the running product without a special-case branch.
examples.trace:
seed: maxHere=-2, minHere=-2, best=-2
i=1 x=0:
  candMax = max(0, -2*0=0, -2*0=0) = 0
  candMin = min(0, 0, 0) = 0
  maxHere=0, minHere=0, best=max(-2,0)=0
i=2 x=-1:
  candMax = max(-1, 0*-1=0, 0*-1=0) = 0
  candMin = min(-1, 0, 0) = -1
  maxHere=0, minHere=-1, best=max(0,0)=0
return 0

examples.note: The killer case — two negatives cancel. The minHere line keeps the highly-negative running product alive long enough for the second negative to flip it back positive.
examples.trace:
seed: maxHere=-2, minHere=-2, best=-2
i=1 x=3:
  candMax = max(3, -2*3=-6, -2*3=-6) = 3
  candMin = min(3, -6, -6) = -6 ← critical: keep -6 in minHere
  maxHere=3, minHere=-6, best=max(-2,3)=3
i=2 x=-4:
  candMax = max(-4, 3*-4=-12, -6*-4=24) = 24 ← the flip!
  candMin = min(-4, -12, 24) = -12
  maxHere=24, minHere=-12, best=max(3,24)=24
return 24

sections.why: Tracing surfaces three things. (1) The `[-2, 3, -4]` case is the textbook demonstration of why min tracking matters — without minHere=-6 kept alive at i=1, the i=2 step couldn't flip to 24. That's the whole reason this problem exists as a separate puzzle from Kadane. (2) The zero-reset trace validates that 'start fresh at nums[i]' handles zeros without a guard. (3) The first canonical case shows the answer can lock in early and stay best, even as subsequent extensions degrade — that's why we update `best` after every step, not just at the end.

sections.title: 5. Edge cases to mention
sections.prompt: What inputs would trip up a careless implementation?
sections.say:
"Before I declare it done, let me think about edges:
• Single element `[5]` or `[-3]` — seed sets maxHere=minHere=best=nums[0], loop doesn't run, returns nums[0]. Works for both signs.
• All positives `[1, 2, 3, 4]` — minHere stays small (it's the running min, which is just 1 after step 0), maxHere monotonically grows, answer is the product of the whole array.
• All negatives `[-2, -3, -4]` — alternating signs flip max and min; odd-length all-negative arrays exclude the most-negative element from the answer. Trace: at i=2, candMax = max(-4, -3*-4=12, 6*-4=-24) = 12. Returns 12 (the pair, not the triple).
• All zeros — every step computes max(0, 0, 0) = 0, returns 0.
• Single negative surrounded by zeros `[0, -1, 0]` — best stays 0 (we'd never pick the standalone -1 over standalone 0). Verified by the trace.
• Float precision — products can lose precision fast; on (-0.5, 0.5)-style floats the answer might drift. Out of scope for integer inputs.
• Integer overflow — products can blow past `2^53` faster than sums (logarithmic growth). For large positive inputs, switch to BigInt or note that the answer fits in the spec's bound."
sections.why: The all-negative case is the senior signal — most candidates don't trace it and assume 'product of all = the answer', which is wrong for odd-length all-negative arrays. The single-negative-with-zeros case validates that we never accidentally choose a worse-than-zero answer when a zero is available. The integer-overflow note ties back to the product-vs-sum distinction: products explode much faster, and naming that shows you've actually considered the data type.

sections.title: 6. Complexity & wrap-up
sections.prompt: How would you defend the complexity claim?
sections.say:
"Time is `O(n)` — single pass, constant work per element (three multiplies, two min/max, three assignments, one global max update). Space is `O(1)` — just three scalars: maxHere, minHere, best.

The brute force was `O(n²)`; the two-track Kadane variant collapses it to `O(n)` because the only state we need to carry across the gap from index `i-1` to `i` is the max AND min product ending at `i-1`. That's it — no array, no history.

The critical implementation detail to call out: compute `candMax` and `candMin` from the SAME old `maxHere` and `minHere` before assigning either back. If you write `maxHere = candMax; minHere = ...` and the second line still references `maxHere`, you've already corrupted it. Use the two-scalar `candMax/candMin` pattern.

The template extends to: Maximum Sum Subarray (the original Kadane, single-track because addition doesn't flip sign); Maximum Product of Three Numbers (sort, max of `last_three.product` vs `first_two_negative * last_positive` — the same negative-flip insight); Maximum Sum Circular Subarray (Kadane plus a min-subarray-sum trick for the wrap-around case)."
sections.why: Repeating the same-source-before-assign warning in the complexity section is the move — interviewers love seeing you flag the bug *before* writing the code, then explain the two-scalar fix. The Kadane vs. Kadane-product contrast is the load-bearing template insight: 'addition doesn't flip sign, multiplication does' is what tells you when to use single-track vs. two-track. That generalizes to any associative-but-sign-volatile operation.

walkthrough.intro: Step through the two-track Kadane variant. Watch maxHere and minHere swap roles whenever a negative number multiplies in — that's the whole reason a single-track max can't solve this.
trace: yield { line: 1, label: `enter — nums=${JSON.stringify(nums)}`, state: { nums } };
const dp = [{ max: maxHere, min: minHere }];
yield { line: 5, label: `seed: maxHere=minHere=best=nums[0]=${nums[0]}`, state: { nums, maxHere, minHere, best, dp: [...dp] } };
yield { line: 6, label: `outer step: i=${i}, x=${x}`, state: { nums, i, x, maxHere, minHere, best, dp: [...dp] } };
const candMax = Math.max(x, maxHere * x, minHere * x);
const candMin = Math.min(x, maxHere * x, minHere * x);

yield { line: 10, label: `candidates: x=${x}, maxHere*x=${maxHere * x}, minHere*x=${minHere * x} → candMax=${candMax}, candMin=${candMin}`, state: { nums, i, x, maxHere, minHere, candMax, candMin, best, dp: [...dp] } };
yield { line: 12, label: `commit: maxHere=${maxHere}, minHere=${minHere}`, state: { nums, i, x, maxHere, minHere, best, dp: [...dp], lastFilled: i } };
yield { line: 13, label: `best = max(prev_best, maxHere) = ${best}`, state: { nums, i, x, maxHere, minHere, best, dp: [...dp] } };
yield { line: 15, label: `return best = ${best}`, state: { nums, maxHere, minHere, best, dp: [...dp], returns: best } };

notes: A negative element flips min ↔ max, so a Kadane-style single-track DP fails here — you need both rails.
Compute new max and min from the SAME (old) maxHere/minHere — don't overwrite maxHere before computing minHere.
Including `x` alone in the max/min handles the reset case (e.g. when the previous product was zero or the wrong sign).
reference.crux: Track BOTH the running max and min product ending here — a negative flips min into the new max; each is max/min of (x, maxHere·x, minHere·x).
cruxDistractors: Run single-track Kadane on the product (carry only the running max, reset when it drops) — silently wrong on [-2,3,-4] because it loses the negative that later flips positive.
Count the negatives: if even, multiply the whole array; if odd, drop the array up to or after the worst negative and take the larger side — breaks once zeros split the array.
Take the absolute value of every element, run Kadane for the max product of magnitudes, then reattach the sign at the end.

alternates.label: Explicit DP arrays (maxArr[] + minArr[])
alternates.when: Reach for this when the interviewer asks 'walk me through the DP recurrence' or wants to see the full table for didactic clarity. Same O(n) time but O(n) space — the two scalars become two arrays indexed by i, making each step's dependency on i-1 explicit at the cost of memory. Useful as a stepping stone: write this first, then optimize to the rolling-scalar version by noting only `i-1` is ever read. Some interviewers prefer it because the same-source-before-assign trap disappears (each cell reads only from the prior cell).
notes: Each row depends only on row i-1, which is the textbook signal that the array can be collapsed to two rolling scalars — that's the optimization back to the canonical.
No same-source-before-assign hazard here: maxArr[i] reads maxArr[i-1] (untouched), so the order of the max/min assignments doesn't matter.
Best teaching version of the recurrence: write this on the whiteboard first, then point at 'we only ever read i-1' to motivate the space-optimized scalars.

questions.q: Why does Kadane's single-track DP (max only) fail for product subarray?
options: Kadane's reset-to-zero condition (drop the running sum when it goes negative) doesn't have a product equivalent
A negative element can flip the running min into the new max
Zeros in the array break the running max in a way that's irrecoverable without backtracking
Multiplication is not associative on floats, so the running product order matters and Kadane assumes associativity
questions.explain: The most negative running product is one negative element away from being the largest. In `[-2, 3, -4]` the min rail holds -6 going into the last element, and -6 × -4 = 24 is the answer — a max-only track would have thrown that -6 away.

questions.q: Why include `x` itself in the max/min of the three candidates?
options: It seeds Math.max so the three-arg form doesn't fall back to -Infinity on the first iteration
Handles the reset case — when the previous product is zero or the wrong sign, start fresh at x
It guarantees the answer is at least one element, satisfying the non-empty subarray constraint
It anchors the index — without `x`, the recurrence loses track of which position the running max ends at
questions.explain: The best subarray ending at i may be x on its own. In `[2, 3, -2, 4]` the -2 step's two products are `maxHere*x = -12` and `minHere*x = -6` — both worse than -2 itself, so the bare `x` is what restarts the max rail instead of dragging a negative product forward. After a zero the products are both 0, and only `x` can revive the rails.

questions.q: What is the space complexity of the optimal solution?
questions.explain: Three scalars carry the whole state — `maxHere`, `minHere` and `best`. No dp array is ever allocated, so nothing scales with `nums.length`.

questions.q: Why must you compute candMax and candMin from the SAME maxHere/minHere before assigning?
options: Otherwise Math.max and Math.min would each get called twice on the same arg, doubling the comparator cost
If you overwrite maxHere first, candMin sees the new value and computes the wrong product
Because const re-binding inside the loop body would throw in strict mode if the order is swapped
Because the cand variables are hoisted into the outer scope, so a swap captures stale references
questions.explain: Both new candidates depend on the OLD pair. Overwriting one early corrupts the other.
